value: during exposure, wild-caught bank voles ranked the weasel-cue treatment as the greatest risk, with the rabbit and control treatments having similar ranks
units: rank of risk by proportion of millet harvested from a patch (rank 1 = greatest risk)
method: laboratory interview-chamber foraging trials: each vole interviewed for nine nights in systems of three sand-filled millet patches, each with a roof cue box holding weasel bedding (wood shavings, urine, hair and faeces), rabbit bedding (sham control) or nothing (control); 2-hour foraging round per night; proportion of millet harvested per patch compared by Friedman tests of concordance within chronological stages (pre-exposure, during exposure, post-exposure)
conditions: 39 analysed voles (40 trapped, 20 male and 20 female; one female removed for signs of pregnancy), trapped in forests around the Konnevesi Research Station and near Oulainen (Finland) and held a few weeks in the laboratory; food withdrawn four days before the experiment; cue boxes 11 x 11 x 6 cm with fresh bedding daily, no dose or mass stated and the paper does not say whether weasel or rabbit bedding came from wild or captive animals; treatments randomised in system and hour of interview; during-exposure nights a live least weasel was caged beside one room of two systems expanded to four rooms, so the ranking is under live predator presence, not bedding odour alone

source.authors: Bleicher SS, Ylönen H, Käpylä T, Haapakoski M
source.title: Olfactory cues and the value of information: voles interpret cues based on recent predator encounters

quote: During the exposure, the voles ranked the weasel-cue treatment as the greatest risk with the rabbit and controls having similar ranks.
note: Classification: behavioural response (foraging patch use) of wild-caught voles to predator-bedding odour in the presence of a live caged predator; no chemoreceptor is identified and no odour-only effect is shown for the exposure stage. Test statistics for this stage (Table 1): Friedman chi-square 6.764, df 2, P = 0.034, Kendall W = 0.087. Contrary and secondary results from the same paper: Friedman tests found no main effect of cue treatment on foraging tenacity (chi-square 3.273, P = 0.195, W = 0.042) while chronology (P < 0.001) and the chronology x treatment interaction (P < 0.001) were significant; concordance in risk assessment was found only during and post exposure (the sentence before this one in the paragraph), not pre-exposure; post-exposure voles ranked the control least dangerous and avoided rabbit and weasel cues similarly; vole activity was lower in all patch types when the live weasel was present and activity in rabbit (sham) patches was highest on exposure nights; mean rank 1.31 during exposure versus 2.46 pre-exposure and 2.23 post-exposure (the paper's wording: the lower the rank the greater the risk; the Methods do not define rank); males harvested less overall than females (16.7% vs 21.9%); mean harvest in control patches rose from 19.4% to 30.1% after exposure. The quote prints no comma between 'risk' and 'with' (reader confirmed). The effect is small (W = 0.087). value: no pre-existing preference for any of the odour cues tested (null result)
units: proportion of first 10 hole choices (0.5 = no preference)
method: hole-choice test: half the holes baited with a bag of wax pellets (about 0.001 g each, 10% odour substance by weight) of methyl salicylate (MeSA), methyl jasmonate (MeJA) or lavender and no mealworm, the other holes non-baited controls with bags of pellets without odour substance; visits recorded for 10 min and the first 10 choices used to estimate preference; GLMM analysis, n = 34 birds
conditions: 35 adult great tits caught in mist nets outside the breeding season (November 2019 to February 2020) at two urban and three rural localities in Sweden and released at the capture sites after the experiments (permit 5.2.18-04716/2018, Swedish regional ethical permit board); n = 34 in the initial-preference model; each bag held five pellets, cut to one pellet per bag for MeSA and lavender after the first group of birds appeared to avoid them, so pellet number differed between groups; vanilla was not tested for initial preference; the setting of the holes (aviary or field) was not read from the page

quote: We found no evidence that great tits had any pre-existing preference for any of the odor cues tested (…).
note: Cut: the quote ends with '(…)' for the printed parenthetical '(Table 1; mean preference ± SD for MeSA = 0.52 ± 0.19, MeJA = 0.5 ± 0.15 and lavender = 0.57 ± 0.15)', which is read from the reader's return and carries the means (0.52, 0.50, 0.57 against a no-preference value of 0.5; the odours were methyl salicylate, methyl jasmonate and lavender). Classification: protocol-specific null for pre-existing odour preference in wild-caught great tits; the odour presence is a cue to birds with food-hole choice, no receptor is identified, and a null at this dose does not show the birds cannot smell the compounds. Secondary results from the same paper, not the null: in the associative learning test (n = 24 for the olfactory cues) MeSA was learned slower than MeJA (GLMM, p = 0.007) and vanilla (p = 0.02), with a non-significant tendency against lavender (p = 0.079); birds did not learn herbivore-induced plant volatiles faster than neutral plant odours, and the authors report no differences in learning speed among olfactory, visual and multimodal cues; the sentence after the quote reads that birds learned MeSA significantly slower than MeJA and vanilla, and possibly lavender (Figure 1 and Table 1).
